"Gurpreet, the haldi is in the garden. In July. In Mumbai."
"I know, Simran. My mother has dreamed of that garden for years."
"Then let's keep the garden. But what's our plan if it pours?"
Gurpreet sighed. "Honestly? I was hoping it won't."
"Hoping isn't a plan. The society hall downstairs is free that morning. What if we book it as a backup? Just in case."
"And move everything down at the last minute?"
"Not everything. The haldi things are in two trunks. We tell your cousins now that if it rains, they carry the trunks and the chairs. We keep a little money aside for surprises too, like extra tarpaulin or a late tempo."
"You've thought about this a lot."
"I've lived through three monsoon weddings."
That Saturday it rained at seven. By eight, the haldi was set up in the hall, cousins dripping and laughing. Gurpreet's mother smiled anyway.

Vaibhav wanted the mehendi on the riverside lawn in Guwahati, in the middle of June. I remember thinking, in June, it's not if it rains, it's when.
So I didn't argue about the lawn. I just asked myself: what would we do at four in the afternoon if the sky opened? The answer was the community hall two streets away. We booked it for the same evening and paid a small deposit. We also set aside a bit of money in an envelope, labelled "surprises", for things like extra umbrellas or a second auto.
My friends thought I was being gloomy.
At three-thirty that day, black clouds came over the river. Vaibhav looked at me and said, "Hall?" I said, "Hall."
By four-thirty, the mehendi artists were set up indoors, and the music was playing again. The envelope paid for plastic sheets and a lot of chai.
— Jaya

The printer needed the final guest count by nine the next morning, and at eleven at night Ishita and Karthik were shouting in the kitchen of their rented flat in Chennai.
"Your mother added thirty people today!"
"And your father added twenty-five last week!"
Karthik slammed the list on the counter. Then he stopped, breathed, and sat on the floor. "This isn't working."
Ishita sat next to him. After a minute, she said, "Let's stop adding and make a rule. A cap. Two hundred and fifty."
"And exceptions?"
"Only if someone we'd actually miss would be hurt. And we both have to agree."
They went through the list quietly with that rule. Two exceptions made it; the rest didn't.
At midnight they wrote a message to both families: the cap, the reason (the hall size and their savings), and a thank-you. They sent the count to the printer at eight fifty.

The fight in Darshan and Aditi's Pune flat started over a single name: Aditi's college friend's parents.
"You don't even know them!"
"You invited your entire gym!"
Aditi grabbed her keys and walked out. Darshan sat on the balcony, angry and then just tired.
She came back an hour later with two cups of tea. "Can we start again? Not the list. The rules."
They agreed on a cap of two hundred. Then an exception rule: someone outside the cap comes only if both of them would feel the person's absence at the wedding. Not one, both.
Suddenly the list was easy. The gym friends were out. The college friend's parents, who had once fed Aditi for a month, were in; Darshan agreed after hearing that.
On Sunday they visited both sets of parents together and explained: the cap, the rule, the reasons. Aditi's mother grumbled, then said, "Fine. At least it's fair."

Dear Zubin,

You asked how Sadia and I are handling money after the wedding. Short answer: better than I expected, because of one evening.
Two weeks after we got back, she said, "Let's put everything on the table. All of it." I was nervous. I had my education loan EMI, which I'd only mentioned vaguely. She had her own loan, and a small savings account from her first job that I didn't know about.
We wrote it all on one sheet: both salaries, both EMIs, what we'd saved, and what we each wanted in five years. Hers: a small flat. Mine: finishing my loan early and one trip abroad.
Seeing it together changed the conversation. We stopped guessing about each other and started asking, "What can we do as a team?"
We're meeting a financial adviser next month to look at options together.

Irfan

Bidisha, you asked how Vivek and I stopped fighting about money in our first year. I'll tell you exactly what we did.
I'm Kashish, and I used to be the person who hid bank messages. Not because anything was wrong, just habit.
About three months after the wedding, we had a silly argument about a phone he bought. I realised we were each guessing about the other's money. So one Sunday I said, "Let's write everything down. Everything."
It took two hours. His salary, mine. His education loan EMI, which was bigger than I'd thought. My savings, which were smaller than he'd assumed. Then what we wanted: he wanted a car in two years, I wanted to do a master's.
Once it was all on one page, we weren't arguing about a phone anymore. We were two people looking at one plan.
Honestly, that page saved our first year.

They'd worked it out the night before. One joint account for rent, electricity and groceries. Each would put in a share matched to their salary: Mohit earned more, so he'd put in more. Whatever was left stayed in their own separate accounts, no questions asked.

"Yes," Sangeeta said. "And the standing instructions from both salaries on the first."
The queue behind them grew. Mohit's pen ran out. Disha lent him hers.

Bhavna, you asked how Rhea and I stopped having those big money fights. Honestly, it's thirty minutes and a pot of tea.
In our first year, we'd only talk about money when something went wrong. I'd see a big charge and get upset, or she'd find out I'd paid for my brother's trip without telling her. Every conversation felt like an ambush.
So we made a rule. The first Sunday of every month, after breakfast, we sit at the table with the expenses from the month. Thirty minutes, no longer. What we spent, anything coming up, anything worrying either of us.
Last month Rhea said she was thinking about a new laptop. Because it came up at the meeting, we planned for it together. No surprise charge, no fight.
It sounds boring, I know. I'm Siddharth, and I never thought I'd say this, but boring is great.

When Valentina and Emeka got married in Madrid, their friends were buying flats and cars. They made a different first decision.
On their first Sunday as a married couple, at the kitchen table, they added up what they spent in a normal month: rent, food, transport, phone. Then they agreed that before any big goal, they would build a reserve worth six months of that, kept in a savings account they could get to quickly.
It took them almost two years. Valentina moved to a cheaper phone plan. Emeka cycled to work in spring.
Last October, Emeka's company announced layoffs. For three weeks nobody knew who would stay. Emeka couldn't sleep.
Valentina put the reserve statement on the fridge with a magnet. "Look. Six months. Whatever happens, we're fine for a while."
He kept his job in the end. But he still remembers how that piece of paper made him breathe.

qa.q: How long did it take Valentina and Emeka to build the reserve?
qa.a: Almost two years.

qa.q: How did Emeka feel during the three weeks of layoff uncertainty?
qa.a: Emeka was anxious and couldn't sleep, then felt calmer and reassured when he saw the reserve statement.

qa.q: What else could Valentina and Emeka do now that the scare has passed?
qa.a: They could talk together about their next big goal, and speak to a qualified adviser if they want help comparing options.

qa.q: How did the reserve look to Valentina during the layoff scare?
qa.a: Valentina felt steady enough to comfort Emeka, because the reserve gave them time whatever happened.

grounding: It shows a couple choosing to hold six months of expenses in an accessible account before big goals, which lets them get through a job scare without borrowing.

passage:
The staff canteen at the Bhubaneswar hospital was nearly empty when Rukmini, a staff nurse, sat down across from her husband Arnab, who worked in the hospital's accounts office.
"The trust announced a hiring freeze and job cuts in admin," Arnab said quietly. "My section is on the list for review."
Rukmini put her tea down. Then she took a breath. "Arnab, remember the first year? We said, no flat, no car, until we had six months of our expenses in the account we can use any time."
"I remember. You made us cancel the trip to Darjeeling."
"And it's there now. Six months."
They sat for a moment. Arnab's shoulders came down a little.
Three weeks later, he was told his post would be cut. It took him four months to find a new job at a college. They didn't borrow from anyone. They didn't even touch the last two months of the reserve.

qa.q: How long did it take Arnab to find a new job?
qa.a: It took him four months.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he first told Rukmini about the job cuts, and what changed?
qa.a: He was anxious and tense, speaking quietly, but his shoulders came down a little when she reminded him of the reserve, showing some relief.

qa.q: What else could the couple do after Arnab found the new job?
qa.a: They could talk together about rebuilding the reserve and their next goals, and ask a qualified adviser if they want help with options.

qa.q: How did the reserve look to Rukmini during the uncertain months?
qa.a: Rukmini could stay steady and reassure Arnab, since the reserve they built early meant they could get through without borrowing.

grounding: It shows a couple building six months of expenses in an easy-to-reach account before big goals, which helps them through a job loss without borrowing.
